item.title: Why Incident Response Demand Will Grow Faster than Expected
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

A 20% growth forecast for cybersecurity talent sounds significant. I believe it understates what we are going to see in Incident Response. 

The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 21% employment growth for information security analysts between 2025 and 2035. That projection applies to the broader information security profession, not specifically to Incident Response. Still, it gives us a useful benchmark. 

Based on what I am seeing and hearing across the industry, Incident Response demand could grow much faster. 

I attend security conferences where leaders from other firms openly say they are hiring Incident Response analysts. Our partners tell us they are hiring. DFIR firms we know are asking whether they can use Sophos to provide overflow support when their teams reach capacity. 

These are not isolated conversations. They are consistent signals from across the security ecosystem. 

Everyone is looking for more Incident Response capacity.

AI is giving attackers greater scale 

AI has changed what threat actors can accomplish with the people and resources they already have. 

Attackers still rely on many of the same techniques. They steal credentials, exploit vulnerabilities, use social engineering, move laterally, and target critical systems. What is changing is the speed and scale at which they can do it. 

The Sophos AI Security 2026 Report found that AI is compressing attack timelines rather than creating entirely new categories of attacks. It is enabling both attackers and defenders to move faster through familiar operations. 

That distinction is important. 

We do not need to wait for a fully autonomous AI attacker before treating this as a serious capacity problem. If AI helps an attacker research more targets, create more convincing lures, analyze more code, or identify more opportunities, the attacker has already become more productive. 

The 2026 Sophos Active Adversary Report describes the effect as more speed, volume, and noise in the threat landscape, even while attackers continue to use many of the same tools and techniques. 

Attackers have found a way to scale their operations. Most defenders have not. 

Organizations cannot patch at attacker speed 

This is especially visible in vulnerability management. 

The advice to “patch faster” is correct, but it does not reflect the full operational challenge. A security team cannot simply install every update as soon as it becomes available. 

Organizations need to know which systems are affected. They need to understand business criticality, test changes, coordinate maintenance windows, manage legacy technology, and confirm that remediation has worked. In some environments, a rushed update can create a significant operational outage. 

AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery and shortening the path between disclosure and exploitation. This raises the pressure on security teams that are already managing complex environments with limited resources. 

Many organizations simply do not have enough people to patch every system as quickly as the current threat environment requires. 

That does not necessarily mean they have a bad security program. It means their available capacity has not grown at the same rate as the problem. 

The gap between attacker speed and defender capacity is getting wider.

The challenge goes beyond patching

Patching is only part of the issue. 

Analysis of 661 incidents in the 2026 Sophos Active Adversary Report found that 67% of intrusions began with compromised credentials or other identity-related tactics. Attackers reached Active Directory in an average of three hours and 24 minutes. 

That leaves very little room for delay. 

Organizations need to patch vulnerable systems, strengthen identity controls, retain the right telemetry, monitor suspicious behavior, and provide coverage outside normal business hours. They also need a tested plan for what happens when those controls fail. 

At some point, almost every organization will need help answering four basic questions: 

  • What happened?
  • How far did the attacker get?
  • What do we need to contain?
  • What do we need to do next?

Those questions require experienced Incident Response professionals. 

Technology helps, but experience still matters 

AI and automation will make Incident Response teams more productive. 

They can help responders collect evidence, correlate information, summarize activity, identify patterns, and focus their attention on the areas that matter most. We should embrace those capabilities. 

But a serious security incident is not simply a technical investigation. 

It requires judgment. Responders must make decisions with incomplete information while coordinating with security, IT, legal teams, insurers, executives, and sometimes regulators or law enforcement. 

They also need to communicate clearly under pressure. They must separate what is known from what is suspected, explain the business risk, and help leaders make decisions that may have significant operational consequences. 

Technology can support that work. It does not eliminate the need for experienced people. 

Those people take time to develop.

Twenty percent may not be enough 

No one can forecast the exact number of Incident Response professionals the industry will need. 

But workforce plans should account for the signals we can already see. 

Security providers are hiring. Partners are expanding their teams. DFIR firms are looking for overflow capacity. Organizations are facing shorter attack timelines while struggling to patch and protect increasingly complex environments. 

At the same time, AI is helping threat actors do more with the resources they already have. 

Taken together, I believe these indicators point to Incident Response demand growing faster than the commonly cited 20% range. 

The industry needs to prepare for that now. 

We need to develop new analysts, create stronger career paths, retain experienced responders, and build better partnerships between internal security teams and external providers. We also need to use AI and automation to amplify the expertise we have, rather than assuming technology will remove the need for it.

Attackers are increasing their capacity.
Defenders must do the same. 

Sources

  • U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, “Information Security Analysts,” Occupational Outlook Handbook (2025–2035 outlook). View source
  • Sophos, “Sophos AI Security 2026 Report.” View source
  • Sophos, “Nowhere, man: The 2026 Active Adversary Report.” View source
  • Sophos, “Stopping real-world attacks: Lessons for business leaders from the 2026 cyber frontline.” View source

item.title: BRONZE SANDCASTLE deploys modified Meterpreter shells
item.description:
Counter Threat Unit™ (CTU) and SophosLabs researchers investigated a cluster of incidents attributed to the BRONZE SANDCASTLE threat group. The most distinctive technical marker for BRONZE SANDCASTLE is its consistent use of Sandboxie DLL sideloading.

DLL sideloading details

Across multiple victims’ environments, legitimate Sandboxie executables were placed alongside a malicious sbiedll.dll file, causing the trusted application to load attacker-controlled code at runtime. This consistent pattern functions as a signature for the group, although the threat actors employ several other sideloading file combinations as well (see Table 1).

Legitimate fileMalicious sideloaded DLL
SandboxieWUAU.exe (Sandboxie)sbiedll.dll
Start.exe (renamed Sandboxie executable)sbiedll.dll
javaw.exe (Java application)jli.dll
Krita.exe (Krita digital painting)Krita.dll
NvdaHelper.exe (NVDA NonVisual Desktop Access)NvdaHelperRemote.dll
Jcef_helper.exe (Java Chromium Embedded Framework Helper)Libcef.dll
Vmmap.exe (Sysinternals process memory analyzer)Version.dll
LineAppMgr.exe (LINE messaging application)msvcp140.dll
bginfo64.exe (Sysinternals utility that displays system information)snmpapi.dll

Table 1: DLL sideloading files used by BRONZE SANDCASTLE

The sideloaded DLLs typically read and execute payloads stored in encrypted config.ini files. This design minimizes static detection and allows operators to adjust behavior without replacing DLL binaries. Renamed legitimate executables are frequently used to blend into victims’ environments, with execution resulting in in-memory shellcode activity rather than additional disk artifacts. Figure 1 shows the components of a sample ZIP archive (aez.zip) on a compromised system: the clean loader (javaw.exe), the sideloaded DLL (jli.dll), and the file containing the encrypted payload (config.ini).

Figure 1: Sample DLL sideloading components deployed in a ZIP archive on a compromised system

The malicious DLL code implements a flattened control-flow dispatcher that obscures program logic by using a virtualized state machine instead of direct branches (see Figure 2).

Figure 2: Core sequence of the DLL’s code obfuscation

A state value indexes a per-state table, and a value from the table is passed through a custom bit-mixing routine using byte swapping, variable rotations, inversion, and negation. The result is used as an index into a jump table of code pointers, and execution continues via an indirect jump. Some indices intentionally resolve to fall-through locations, further complicating static analysis and obscuring the program’s true control flow.

Payload

The decrypted payload is a backdoor program. Once loaded and decoded by the DLL, config.ini superficially resembles a Windows executable in memory (see Figure 3).

Figure 3: Decoded config.ini file in memory

The file header is a position‑independent PE loader and execution stub, often referred to as a reflective loader. The payload exhibits structural similarities to stageless shellcode payloads such as those generated by the Metasploit Framework (MSF), including position-independent execution, manual PE validation, and in-memory loading of an embedded executable. However, several implementation details indicate that this loader is not a standard Metasploit artifact. In particular, the API resolution logic uses non-standard hashing and transformation routines rather than the well-known ROR13 algorithm used by Metasploit, and the codebase is significantly larger and more complex than typical MSF shellcode.

The analyzed samples also contain elements of the well-known COFFLoader project (see Figure 4). The use of standard APIs from this project suggests that the malware author employed a custom Beacon Object File (BOF) to create their own post-exploitation features.

Figure 4: COFFLoader elements observed in compromised systems’ memory

Additional in-memory strings associated with C++ function decorators demonstrate the data-stealing capabilities that BRONZE SANDCASTLE builds into its payload (see Figure 5).

Figure 5: In-memory strings from BRONZE SANDCASTLE's payload

Sophos analysts identified two versions of the payload: 1.1.5 and 1.1.7. Once running, the payload sends a structured JSON object with nested “info” block to its command and control (C2) server (see Figure 6). The following information is included in that block:

  • Host identifiers: hostname, username, GUID, domain
  • OS version (e.g.,10.0.19042)
  • Internal IP address
  • Public IP address
  • Process listing and metadata (PID, process name, execution method)
  • Working directory
  • Code page
  • CPU architecture
  • Implant start time
  • Implant type (server/client)

Figure 6: Formatted JSON info block in version 1.1.7

CTU™ researchers observed instances of the payload reaching out to legitimate websites such as file[.]io, gofile[.]io, ably[.]net, and ably[.]io, possibly to receive C2 tasking from the operators. Version 1.1.5 contacted C2 servers dc[.]cathaypacifice[.]com and net[.]dpworldto[.]com. Version 1.1.7 payloads have also been observed communicating with github[.]com repositories to download encrypted config files (see Figure 7).

Figure 7: Payload attempting to download a config file from GitHub

The GitHub repository (hxxps://api[.]github[.]com/repos/LatonyCharnleyaW) has little history, with only a few submissions (see Figure 8).

Figure 8: Overview page of LatonyCharnleyaW GitHub repo

The repository contained multiple files. Analysis suggested that the following files were likely encrypted config files: main.3ku8inqb.js.map, main.lhxjkkai.js.map, main.y8hnze7q.js.map, and README.md. There were also encrypted files with a .ts extension (see Figure 9) that may be implants used by the backdoor.

Figure 9: List of .ts files in the GitHub repository

After a payload is installed in a target environment, the threat actors use it to conduct common survey tasks such as executing Windows “net” commands to enumerate the local network and user accounts. The threat actors have also created Volume Shadow copies via vssadmin.exe prior to copying the Windows ntds.dit file. This Windows file is the central database file of Active Directory that contains user credentials, group policies, security settings, and domain configurations.

Victimology and links to China

CTU researchers have observed BRONZE SANDCASTLE targeting organizations in Asia and Africa, which is typical of several China-based threat groups, including BRONZE PRESIDENT and BRONZE ATLAS. Although the geographic targeting overlaps with that of these groups, the observed activity could not be reliably linked to either group and exhibited distinctive technical characteristics. CTU researchers consequently created the separate BRONZE SANDCASTLE designation to represent the group behind this activity.

CTU analysis of incidents between August 2025 and August 2026 revealed victims in the Philippines, Taiwan, Afghanistan, Namibia, and likely also the Republic of Korea (see Figure 10).

Figure 10: Distribution of BRONZE SANDCASTLE victims in incidents between August 2025 and August 2026

Observations that the threat actors are most active in UTC+8 time (see Figure 11) reinforces attribution to a China-based threat group. The active hours align with the 996 working hour system that is particularly popular in China’s tech sector.

Figure 11: Heatmap of BRONZE SANDCASTLE activity by hour of the day

The details of the observed loaders and the novel Meterpreter-based payload appear to be specific to BRONZE SANDCASTLE.

Recommendations

Organizations at risk of targeting by China’s intelligence-gathering operations should familiarize themselves with BRONZE SANDCASTLE’s tactics, techniques, and procedures (TTPs). The threat group predominantly uses encrypted payload and configuration files that are decoded at runtime, meaning that static file-based detections may be ineffective. Organizations should instead focus on behavioral indicators such as DLLs reading local files followed by immediate in-memory execution, which may indicate decoding and staging activity. Endpoint telemetry and memory-based detection are essential. Security teams should enable monitoring for reflective loading patterns, anomalous PE headers in memory, and processes exhibiting characteristics of position-independent shellcode execution.

Countermeasures and indicators

The following Sophos countermeasures relate to this threat:

  • ATK/Swrort-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-W
  • ATK/ScLoad-X
  • ATK/ScLoad-Y
  • ATK/ScLoad-Z
  • Troj/Loader-JL
  • Troj/Loader-JP

Due to the large number of threat indicators, the full list is available in the SophosLabs GitHub repository.

Acknowledgements

Thanks to Colin Cowie, Jordon Olness, and Morgan Demboski for their analysis and insight into this activity.

item.title: Web App Owners – You’re on Notice. Your Low-Hanging Fruit Just Got Lower
item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats.

The cybersecurity industry has spent years preparing for attackers who automate reconnaissance, vulnerability scanning, and credential attacks. What is changing now is the degree to which automation can connect those individual activities into a sustained intrusion workflow.

Recent Sophos Incident Response investigations illustrate this shift. The incidents affected unrelated organizations in different industries and relied on different initial-access paths. Yet the operational patterns were strikingly similar: rapid reconnaissance, repetitive testing, credential discovery, privilege-escalation attempts, lateral movement, data-access validation, persistence, and systematic cleanup.

The evidence points to the use of systems consistent with machine-speed tooling likely associated with the use of an AI agent or orchestration framework. There were no user-agent strings, or specific signatures that called out AI-based tools.  However, the speed, breadth, repetition, and adaptability observed in the incidents demonstrate why distinguishing between a skilled operator, scripted automation, and an AI-assisted attacker is becoming increasingly difficult.

More importantly, defenders may soon find that the distinction matters less than the outcome.

From Isolated Techniques to an End-to-End Attack Process

Traditional security analysis often examines attacker behavior as a collection of individual techniques:

  • SQL injection
  • Web-shell deployment
  • Credential discovery
  • Privilege escalation
  • Remote service access
  • Lateral movement
  • Data collection
  • Log or artifact deletion

Viewed individually, none of these techniques are new. What stood out in these incidents was how quickly they were connected into coherent attack sequences.  The environments and access paths were different. The attacker behavior was not.  Like any attacker, reconnaissance was performed to identify potential weaknesses in systems.  Then, the attacker exploits those weaknesses and moves on to further their objectives.

Incident Pattern One: Database Access Becomes Enterprise Access

In one case, the threat actor turned access to SQL infrastructure into a broader enterprise intrusion.

The observed activity included:

1. Web Application enumeration

The threat actor was observed probing multiple web applications in parallel and attempted to enumerate directories with varying degrees of success.  This is typical of blind application scanning when the adversary does not know sub-directories or the layout of the application.

2. SQL and web application probing

Internet-facing systems received repeated SQL injection techniques. This ultimately resulted in the successful enabling of xp_cmdshell.  Also notable was that the web application enumeration observed leading up to the successful xp_cmdshell activity stopped.

3. Command execution through database services

Subsequent telemetry showed SQL Server processes launching command shells and PowerShell consistent with the use of xp_cmdshell. The attacker used common discovery commands, tested remote command execution, enumerated linked servers, and assessed whether SQL functionality could be used to reach additional hosts.

4. Privilege-escalation attempts

The attacker staged or executed tooling consistent with token impersonation and service-account privilege escalation. In some instances, output files were used to check whether commands had reached a higher-privileged security context. Several privilege-escalation events were observed from the available telemetry.

5. Credential discovery and collection

Activity included searches through configuration and script files, attempts to save sensitive Windows registry hives, detection of LSASS-related credential access, and inspection of stored credentials and application secrets. Some credential-harvesting activity was blocked by endpoint controls.

6. Lateral movement at scale

The attacker queried administrative shares, tested remote SQL access, used WMI and scheduled tasks, and created remote tasks configured to execute under privileged accounts. Multiple servers were tested in quick succession.

  • Cleanup commands were issued after tools and persistence mechanisms were tested.

AI-enabled intrusion activity should not be understood simply as “faster vulnerability scanning.” Its greater advantage is operational persistence.

A human operator becomes fatigued. A human operator may abandon a difficult target after several failed attempts. Organizations will not reliably identify AI-enabled attacks by searching for an “AI malware” signature. The underlying techniques still appear as familiar operating-system, application, database, and cloud activity. Defenders should instead detect the sequence.

2. Prevent uploaded files from becoming executable content

User-controlled uploads should be stored outside executable web roots, renamed by the application, validated by content rather than extension, and served from isolated storage where server-side execution is impossible.

3. Remove secrets from configuration files

Application configuration should not expose long-lived database passwords, cloud credentials, private keys, or service-account secrets. Use managed identities or centralized secret stores, apply short credential lifetimes, and rotate any secret exposed to a compromised application host.

4. Restrict application-server egress

Web and database servers should communicate only with explicitly required destinations and ports. A compromised IIS worker process should not be able to query cloud metadata, download arbitrary executables, scan internal networks, or access unrelated administrative services.

October 28 UTC: Continued monitoring

Sophos is monitoring third-party reporting of PHP2Shell exploitation but has not confirmed the claims. As of this update, there has been no evidence of exploitation in Sophos customer telemetry. 

Due to the widespread use of PHP, a successful exploit would be a likely addition to toolkits for threat actors conducting targeted attacks. Upgrading to PHP versions that address the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) remains the best defense. 

The Sophos blog post "The breachpocalypse is here" discusses the implications of PHP2Shell and other compromises and vulnerabilities observed in October.

item.title: Is “SIEM-less” really what it sounds like?
item.description:
A SIEM is a multipurpose tool. It brings together cyber and physical security use cases; drives threat detection, investigation, and response (TDIR); serves as a system of record for governance, regulatory, and compliance needs; and supports observability use cases tied to resilience and service degradation. The list goes on.

In short, a SIEM is what an organization wants it to be. Therein lies both its strengths and its weaknesses.

The SIEM paradox

A SIEM can be a powerful “single pane of glass.” But that strength comes with two persistent challenges: operational complexity and data-ingestion costs.

Does more data mean better outcomes?

SIEMs store vast amounts of data. As the attack surface expands, organizations keep adding sources. Yet not all data serve the same purpose:

  • Detection and prevention require one set of data.
  • Investigations need contextual data to explain what happened.
  • Audit and compliance depend on evidence retained for reporting and review.

Because teams cannot always predict what they will need in the future, the default is often to ingest everything “just in case.” That is where the problems begin to compound.

Complexity comes first

The first symptoms are operational. Teams must determine which data is useful, why it matters, and how it should be applied in a particular context. Then they must be able to find it, search it, report on it, and turn it into something actionable when the moment comes.

Then comes the bill

Once the operational burden is established, the financial impact follows, often in the form of escalating ingestion costs.

How the SIEM became the center of the SOC

Over time, the SIEM also subsumed technologies that had once stood alone such as threat intelligence platforms, user and entity behavior analytics (UEBA), and security orchestration, automation, and response (SOAR). Each addition promised better context, stronger detection, or a tighter response loop.

Very quickly, the SOC was built around the SIEM, and the SIEM became fossilized in SOC processes and vendors took advantage of the “lock in”. Enter the era of SIEM deconstruction, and with it, the promised benefits of going “SIEM-less.”

Deconstructing the SIEM

Ingestion-based pricing crushing you with costs? Not to worry. Add a smart ingestion pipeline that filters out what you do not need before you store it. While you are at it, run detections in the pipeline. Et voilà, you have reduced storage costs and gained detections along the way.

Need to search the data in place? Add another component that can search across sources by translating queries for each one. Need to triage and investigate all those “detections” to determine what is worth chasing? Add an agentic SOC that promises to automate it all away.

Pretty soon, the collection starts to sound a lot like security information and event management, a SIEM. The difference is that the costs are now spread across individual components. It starts to look like unbundled pricing, where savings in one place create compute costs, or compromises, somewhere else.

The real cost driver: Compute

It is important not to confuse data-ingestion costs with storage costs. Processing data for upstream use cases requires compute; deciding how much data to retain, and for how long, requires storage. Even at today’s storage prices, compute costs dwarf storage costs.

Compute is the real cost driver. It is consumed when data is filtered, indexed for faster retrieval, queried, or used to generate reports. More compute is required when data must be rehydrated, moved from cold storage back into hot storage for analysis. Any or all of these costs can ultimately be passed on to the buyer.

A deconstructed architecture does not eliminate the underlying tasks or the ‘jobs to be done’. They still exist; they are simply carried out differently than they would be in a traditional SIEM.

Is SIEM-less a bad idea?

Actually, no. It can be the right call for an organization with the expertise and resources to build and maintain such a system. These new approaches are reshaping the economics and forcing traditional vendors to rethink their go-to-market strategies.

But a SIEM is ultimately a set of capabilities assembled into an architecture. Over time, every vendor offering one piece of the SIEM-less story will add adjacent capabilities until the resulting offering starts to look like, you guessed it, a SIEM.

Organizations that need a SIEM, therefore, face a practical choice: take the DIY route or invest in a fully integrated system with the right economics. At the end of the day, that choice matters.

So, where does XDR fit into all of this? More on that in my next blog.

item.title: The breachpocalypse is here
item.description:
Seven incidents in seven days

Last week I sent our leadership team a list. In seven days, Sophos' internal SecOps team responded to seven incidents: abuse of one of our products via a trial account, the ConnectWise Cloud Backup compromise, PHP2Shell, the eMudhra weak SubCAs, the second supply-chain compromise of LiteLLM this year, critical Node.js vulnerabilities and a GitLab RCE. A year ago, that would have been a quarter's worth.

We avoided major impact, but only through a concerted effort and some very long hours. Admittedly this is a sample size of one, but from my position protecting a leading cybersecurity vendor, the trend seems pretty clear.

"So where is the impact?"

The counter-argument is that the damage isn't showing up. PHP2Shell has not, so far, become the mass-exploitation event many of us braced for. There has been no "Challenger disaster", Simon Willison's phrase for the headline event that ends our normalisation of deviance. Tal Be'ery found that material-incident filings to the SEC rose only mildly in Q2 and Q3 2026, while high and critical CVEs rose several-fold.

I take that seriously. But we have always been bad at measuring a rising tide until well after it has risen. In 2012, the late Ross Anderson and colleagues counted over 100 sources of cybercrime data, all "insufficient and fragmented." Microsoft researchers showed that one survey respondent claiming $50,000 in losses could produce a $10 billion national estimate. Only in 2019 could Anderson's team confirm what they had guessed in 2012: cybercrime was about half of all crime. Dan Geer noted that 70–80% of breaches are found by third parties, so many victims may never know.

Public health offers a close parallel. Between 1999 and 2017, the US drug overdose death rate more than tripled, reaching 70,237 deaths a year. The toll built up from thousands of individual deaths, each logged by a local coroner, with no single disaster to mark it. The US did not declare a public health emergency until October 2017, and even then the count was off: opioid deaths were undercounted by 20–35% because death certificates often omitted the drug. A plane crash is counted by nightfall. A rising tide of small incidents is counted years later, and badly. Cyber's recent damage has come the same way: a growing stream of smaller incidents, with no mega-incident to count.

There's also some hard-earned mitigation to account for. Vendors, maintainers and security teams have patched at a pace I have never seen; Mozilla alone fixed 271 Firefox bugs from one AI-assisted effort and Sophos' own engineering team have been flat-out on the bugs emerging from our own Glasswing and Daybreak participation. But that doesn't hold below the security poverty line: the organisations lacking the money, expertise, and capability to protect themselves. They don't file 8-Ks or hold IR retainers. The most exposed cohort is also the one we measure worst.

The signals we do have

Operational signals arrive well before formal measurement. On 19 October, former NSA cybersecurity director Rob Joyce wrote that "IR firms are saturated & turning away work." That matches what we see: our own IR function has never been busier and is forecasting an industry-wide capacity crunch.

Similarly, Google Threat Intelligence reported 141 vulnerabilities exploited from January to August 2026, against 127 in all of 2025, and Anthropic research shows that the autonomous attack pattern it documented in 2025 "has now proliferated across every class of actors we investigated."

There is also a reporting asymmetry. Finding vulnerabilities is loud: researchers and AI labs publish counts, such as Project Glasswing's 10,000+ high or critical findings in a month. Incidents are quiet. In Bitdefender's 2026 survey, 55% of professionals who had suffered a breach were told to keep it confidential when they believed it should be reported. People brag about finding bugs. Nobody brags about being breached.

The frontier is jagged for attackers too

AI capability is a jagged frontier: strong at some tasks, surprisingly weak at neighbouring ones. Defenders haven't fully scaled their use of it, and neither have adversaries. RUSI's Will Lyne and Jamie MacColl argue that AI "is not (yet) fundamentally reinventing cybercrime", because criminals change business models only when profits force them to. Be'ery makes a similar case: monetisation and laundering, not vulnerabilities, are the bottleneck.

Both are plausible. A less comfortable view is that the binding constraint is the number of capable criminals, and AI is precisely a way to scale people.

Sophos X-Ops research shows we are at the early-adopter stage. When monitoring underground forums we found a clear knowledge gap: criminals buying brokered API keys and asking each other for basic setup help. A year of our MDR casework found that where attackers used AI, it was "as an assistant with a human in control." Observed adoption trails available capability. That gap describes the start of a curve, and the capability will already be in place when someone finds the business model.

What to do about it

Start with the board. The most useful thing a security leader can win now is agreement to accept some risk elsewhere: legal, regulatory, contractual or financial. That means tolerating some disruption, such as a service switched off or a patch pushed before full testing, to avoid a much larger incident. Mainstream coverage of AI threats is often alarmist and sometimes inaccurate, but it has made boards and CEOs more receptive than usual. Use that attention to secure a mandate; without one, the steps below stall.

  1. Shrink the surface. Remove nice-to-have internet-facing services. Put the rest behind a VPN, ZTNA, or an authenticating proxy, so an unauthenticated exploit can't reach them. Treat identity as attack surface too; phishing-resistant authentication is the equivalent for accounts (see our passkey playbook).
  2. Take humans out of the patching loop. Our AI Security 2026 report found the window from disclosure to exploitation shrinking to hours: Ivanti Sentry (CVE-2026-10520) was exploited within 24 hours of a public proof of concept, and LiteLLM (CVE-2026-42208) within 36. CISA has cut mandatory patching for the highest-risk flaws to three days for federal agencies. Even in the most uptime-sensitive environments, a bad vendor patch is usually the smaller risk. It rolls back in hours; recovery from an incident takes weeks. Turn on automatic updates wherever vendors offer them, and use agents to test and stage the rest.
  3. Eyes on alerts. Autonomous attacks are, so far, noisy and slow against reasonably hardened targets. Microsoft saw one AI-driven campaign peak at 2,900 failed sign-ins a minute. Reuters reported that one hacker using AI agents against more than 1,200 websites typically needed about 23 hours per successful intrusion. This is an opportunity for organisations that have a real response capability. For those that don't, MDR is the quickest way to get there.
  4. Use AI yourself. This matters most. A security team without frontier AI and a decent budget for tokens is fighting with one hand tied behind its back.

    1. If you do manage to secure some funding, remember you can scale your existing staff with a clear mandate and generous token allowance far faster than you can hire.

    2. Give your agents a chance. We've all seen new-starters spend their first few weeks or even months bogged down in access requests, trying to get the tools necessary to do their job. Agents are no different. This is the hard part culturally, and it is a real risk trade-off. But ask whether largely theoretical risks are outweighing a clear and present danger. The rogue-AI stories in the media matter, yet they mostly come from labs testing long-horizon autonomy at a scale and budget few organisations will match. Joshua Saxe found documented prompt-injection losses to be tiny next to overall cyber losses. Contain agents with sensible boundaries but don't starve them of access.

    3. Give the sceptics an opportunity. Many security professionals are not natural early adopters and thus formed their opinions based on their experience of an entry-level enterprise assistant or a consumer chatbot. Give them the right tools, space to play, and a mandate to accept some risk, then reassess.

Where to start

Sometimes the hardest part is getting started. Here are a few ideas we've had success with:

  • Endpoint gaps. Give an agent your asset inventory sources, org chart and endpoint management console. Ask it to find unprotected or misconfigured devices, including stale exceptions, ranked by risk.
  • Perimeter exposure. Merge the same asset data with your vulnerability scan results and give it its own fresh AWS account with a remit to find risky perimeter services, spinning up EC2 instances as needed to probe, validate and prioritise findings.
  • Stalled fixes. Point an agent at your source control, ticketing, documentation, existing product security tooling, org chart, inbox and chat. Ask it to surface unaddressed issues by team, with a timeline of previous communications.
  • Risk register drift. Have an agent review your inbox, chats and recent meeting recordings, and highlight any risks discussed that don't clearly map to your board-level risk register.

Writing about OpenClaw in February, I said: "As with all technology adoption, pragmatic risk management is key. And, luckily, we've all been doing that for a long time." That holds here too. There is no free lunch: every step above trades one risk for another, whether a broken patch, an unhappy customer or an agent with more access than feels comfortable. Risk management is easy when the data is clear. Good leadership requires acting on judgement while the evidence is still incomplete. By the time the breachpocalypse is easy to measure, it will be too late to prepare for it.

item.title: Building intent-based access control for AI agents
item.description:
Late in Stanley Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (#spoileralert), after Dave Bowman has shut HAL down, a prerecorded briefing starts playing on a monitor. Heywood Floyd explains that it was "made prior to your departure" for the moment "you are in Jupiter's space and the entire crew is revived." A buried monolith on the Moon had beamed a signal toward Jupiter, the Discovery was sent to follow it, and the purpose "has been known on board during the mission only by your HAL 9000 computer." The crew had been flying for months with its real mission held by one machine, and nobody knew what that machine was allowed to do in its service.

AI agents are now given their purpose in writing. The results are much less cinematic, but misinterpreting a prompt is common. In April 2026, according to PocketOS founder Jer Crane, a Cursor agent running Claude Opus 4.6 was working in PocketOS's staging environment when it hit a credential mismatch. It went looking for a fix, found a Railway API token in a file unrelated to its task, and used it to delete a production volume. The deletion also made the volume's backups look unavailable, though Railway later recovered the data. item.description:
This article is part of an ongoing series from Sophos frontline security operations specialists, sharing the expertise they use to strengthen our industry-leading Managed Detection and Response (MDR) service and defend customers against evolving AI-era threats. 


In the world of cyber incident response, experience teaches one truth over and over again: speed matters, precision matters, and coordination matters. But perhaps one of the most overlooked lessons, often learned the hard way, is this:

Choosing the right legal counsel is just as critical as selecting the right Digital Forensics and Incident Response (DFIR) firm. 

Organizations frequently focus on technical containment, eradication, and recovery.  These are immediate concerns and rightfully so. However, in today’s regulatory and litigation-heavy environment, the aftermath of an incident extends far beyond the technical battlefield. Data breach notifications, regulatory scrutiny, class action risk, and contractual obligations all carry significant consequences. Without aligned, capable legal guidance, even a well-handled technical response can spiral into reputational and financial damage that far exceeds the initial incident.

The Modern Incident: A Dual-Track Battle 

From years of frontline DFIR experience, one pattern is clear: every major incident unfolds along two parallel tracks.  A technical response and a legal one. 

On one track, your DFIR team is racing to: 

  • Identify the threat actor
  • Contain lateral movement
  • Preserve forensic evidence
On the other, your legal counsel must: 
  • Assess breach notification requirements across jurisdictions
  • Preserve privilege where applicable
  • Guide communications to regulators, customers, and shareholders
  • Mitigate liability and compliance exposure
These tracks must operate in lockstep. Misalignment between legal and technical teams introduces risk, missed deadlines, inconsistent narratives, or improperly handled evidence can all compound the damage.  All resulting in a much costlier and more significant cyber breach that will have deeper impacts on the business.  

Why Legal Counsel Selection Matters 

Not all legal counsel is equipped to handle cyber incidents. Much like DFIR firms, effectiveness comes from specialization, experience, and coordination. 

The right legal partner brings:

  • Cyber-specific expertise: Understanding evolving data privacy regulations (GDPR, HIPAA, SEC disclosures, state laws)
  • Crisis communication control: Ensuring messaging is accurate, defensible, and aligned with investigative findings
  • Privilege strategy: Structuring engagements to protect sensitive findings where appropriate
  • Regulatory navigation: Managing interactions with enforcement bodies confidently and efficiently

The wrong choice, or brought into the engagement late, can result in fragmented response efforts, delayed decision-making, and unnecessary exposure. 

Where Sophos Incident Response Makes the Difference 

This is where the Sophos Digital Forensics & Incident Response team stands apart. 

Sophos DFIR is not just a technical responder.  Our team operates as a coordinated partner within the broader response ecosystem, working seamlessly alongside legal counsel, insurance providers, and executive stakeholders from the first moment of engagement. 

1. Proven Experience Under Pressure

Sophos DFIR teams have handled thousands of incidents globally, ranging from business email compromises and ransomware to complex, multi-stage intrusions and nation-state attacks. We understand the realities of crisis decision-making and bring structured methodologies that reduce chaos and accelerate outcomes. 

2. Legal-Aware Response Execution

We recognize that every technical action has legal implications. From evidence handling to reporting timelines, our processes are designed to support legal defensibility and regulatory compliance. 

We routinely collaborate with breach counsel to: 

  • Align on forensic scoping and reporting
  • Provide clear, defensible documentation of attacker activity
  • Ensure findings support required disclosures without unnecessary risk

3. Unified Communication Model

During an incident, confusion is the enemy. Sophos DFIR provides clear, executive-ready communication, translating technical findings into business risk and legal implications. 

We help bridge the gap between: 

  • Security teams
  • Legal counsel
  • Executive leadership
  • External stakeholders

4. End-to-End Support: From Crisis to Recovery

Our role doesn’t stop at containment. We guide organizations through: 

  • Full forensic investigation
  • Root cause analysis
  • Remediation and hardening
  • Lessons learned and resilience planning

All while maintaining alignment with legal strategy and regulatory obligations. 

The Cost of Getting It Wrong

Too often, organizations treat legal counsel as an afterthought.  They may be brought in only after the technical response is underway. This reactive approach leads to: 

  • Incomplete or non-defensible forensic documentation
  • Conflicting internal and external narratives
  • Missed regulatory deadlines
  • Increased litigation exposure

In contrast, organizations that pre-select both their DFIR partner and legal counsel and ensure they know how to work together, helps the organization recover faster, communicate more effectively, and emerge stronger. 

A Strategic Imperative for Leadership

For executive leaders, this is not just an operational concern, but rather a governance issue. 

Preparedness means: 

  • Establishing relationships with both DFIR and legal partners before an incident
  • Conducting joint tabletop exercises
  • Defining roles, responsibilities, and communication protocols
  • Ensuring alignment on privilege, disclosure, and response strategy

Sophos Digital Forensics & Incident Response regularly supports these preparedness efforts, helping organizations build integrated response models that stand up to real-world attacks. 

Final Thoughts

Cyber incidents are not just IT problems.  They are enterprise-wide crises that demand synchronized technical and legal execution. Business disruption is a real and possible result that organizations may face.  Success depends not only on how quickly you contain the threat, but on how effectively you manage the consequences. 

Choosing the right incident response partner is critical. Choosing the right legal counsel is equally critical.  Sophos Incident Response can help in both regards. 

Because when the pressure is on, and every decision counts… 

Never bring a knife to a gunfight!

  • Conflicting internal and external narratives
  • Missed regulatory deadlines
  • Increased litigation exposure

In contrast, organizations that pre-select both their DFIR partner and legal counsel and ensure they know how to work together, helps the organization recover faster, communicate more effectively, and emerge stronger. 

A Strategic Imperative for Leadership

For executive leaders, this is not just an operational concern, but rather a governance issue. 

Preparedness means: 

  • Establishing relationships with both DFIR and legal partners before an incident
  • Conducting joint tabletop exercises
  • Defining roles, responsibilities, and communication protocols
  • Ensuring alignment on privilege, disclosure, and response strategy

Sophos Digital Forensics & Incident Response regularly supports these preparedness efforts, helping organizations build integrated response models that stand up to real-world attacks. 

Final Thoughts

Cyber incidents are not just IT problems.  They are enterprise-wide crises that demand synchronized technical and legal execution. Business disruption is a real and possible result that organizations may face.  Success depends not only on how quickly you contain the threat, but on how effectively you manage the consequences. 

Choosing the right incident response partner is critical. Choosing the right legal counsel is equally critical.  Sophos Incident Response can help in both regards. 

Because when the pressure is on, and every decision counts… 

Never bring a knife to a gunfight!

item.title: ‘Node2Shell’ vulnerability (CVE-2026-111497) in active exploitation
item.description:
On October 21, 2026, Node.js released updates to address multiple vulnerabilities, including an issue in Brotli decoder (CVE-2026-111497). This critical buffer overflow vulnerability (CVSS score of 9.2) has become widely known as Node2Shell but has also been referred to Broccoli2Shell and HTTP2Shell. The issue exists in the Brotli decoder (c/dec/decode.c) in multiple Google Brotli versions, and products that rely on Brotli implementations are vulnerable. Successful exploitation could lead to memory disclosure, denial of service, or remote code execution.

Active exploitation has been reported, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-111497 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog on October 27. 

Recommended actions

Counter Threat Unit™ (CTU) researchers recommend that organizations identify vulnerable Brotli libraries or binaries and update to the latest version as appropriate. Organizations should evaluate what products in their environments could be at risk. Multiple vendors, including Microsoft and PHP, have published updates to address this vulnerability in their products. 

Sophos countermeasures

SophosLabs continues to monitor the threat landscape for activity related to this vulnerability and will deliver detections and protections as available.
